title: Adding a disulfide bridge to an enzyme

stimulus.title: Adding a disulfide bridge to an enzyme
stimulus.html:
Researchers studied an enzyme from a soil bacterium. They made an engineered version in which two amino acids that sit close together in the folded enzyme were each replaced with cysteine, so that the engineered enzyme has one extra disulfide bridge. Samples of the normal and engineered enzymes were held for 10 minutes at one of seven temperatures, then cooled to 25 °C, and the activity of each sample was measured at 25 °C. Activity is given as a percent of the activity of a normal enzyme sample that was never heated. Each value is the average of four separate samples.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe what a disulfide bridge is and which level of protein structure it stabilizes. Explain why a protein that loses its folded shape stops working.

rubric.point: Describes a disulfide bridge as a covalent bond between the sulfur atoms (sulfhydryl groups) of two cysteine side chains that helps hold the tertiary structure (the 3-D shape).
accept: covalent S–S bond between two cysteines that holds the 3-D (tertiary) fold
bond between the –SH groups of two cysteine R groups, stabilizing tertiary structure

rubric.point: Explains that a protein's function depends on its specific 3-D shape, so losing the shape (denaturation) stops it from working.
accept: structure determines function: the unfolded protein no longer has the shape it needs
a denatured enzyme loses the shape that lets it act

parts.sample: A disulfide bridge is a covalent S–S bond between the sulfhydryl groups of two cysteine side chains; it locks parts of the chain together and stabilizes the protein's tertiary structure. A protein works because of its exact 3-D shape, so when it unfolds (denatures) it no longer has the shape its function depends on.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable in this experiment. Justify the researchers' decision to cool every sample to 25 °C before measuring its activity.

rubric.point: Identifies the independent variable as the holding temperature (also accept: the version of the enzyme, normal or engineered).
accept: the temperature at which the samples were held

rubric.point: Justifies that measuring every sample at the same temperature means differences in activity reflect lasting damage done during heating, not the effect of temperature on the measurement itself.
accept: so activity is measured under identical conditions and only the earlier heating differs
so the measured activity shows how much enzyme stayed folded, not how temperature affects the reaction during measurement

parts.sample: The independent variable is the temperature at which each sample was held for 10 minutes. Cooling all samples to 25 °C before measuring means every sample was measured under the same conditions, so any difference in activity shows how much of the enzyme was permanently unfolded by the heating, not how temperature affects the reaction while it is being measured.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Describe how the effect of holding temperature differs between the normal and engineered enzymes. Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between the engineered and normal enzymes' remaining activity at 65 °C.

rubric.point: Describes that both enzymes lose activity at higher temperatures, but the engineered enzyme keeps more activity at each temperature from 55 °C to 70 °C (it loses activity at higher temperatures than the normal enzyme).
accept: the engineered enzyme is more heat-stable: it keeps more activity between 55 and 70 °C
the normal enzyme's activity falls at lower temperatures than the engineered enzyme's

parts.sample: Both enzymes lose activity when held at higher temperatures, but the engineered enzyme keeps much more activity from 55 °C to 70 °C; its activity drops at temperatures roughly 5 to 10 °C higher than the normal enzyme's. At 65 °C the difference is 71 − 18 = 53 percentage points.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Before heating, a sample of the engineered enzyme is treated with a reducing agent, which breaks disulfide bridges, and the reducing agent is then removed while the bridges are kept from re-forming. Predict the activity this sample would keep after 10 minutes at 65 °C, and justify your prediction. Then explain why the engineered and normal enzymes have almost the same activity after 10 minutes at 25 °C.

rubric.point: Predicts that the treated engineered enzyme would keep about as much activity as the normal enzyme at 65 °C, or less (about 18% or lower, much less than 71%).
accept: much lower than 71%, similar to or below the normal enzyme

rubric.point: Justifies that without the extra disulfide bridge, the engineered enzyme's fold is no longer locked by that covalent bond, so heat unfolds it at about the same temperatures as the normal enzyme.
accept: the extra bridge is what made it more heat-stable; breaking it removes the advantage
with no extra covalent bridge holding the fold, heat unfolds it like the normal enzyme

rubric.point: Explains that at 25 °C neither enzyme unfolds, and the extra bridge does not change the working shape, so both keep their full activity.
accept: at 25 °C both stay folded in their working shape
the extra bridge stabilizes the shape without changing it, so activity is normal when nothing unfolds

parts.sample: The treated engineered enzyme would keep only about 18% of its activity at 65 °C, close to the normal enzyme, or even less if its other natural bridges were broken too. The extra disulfide bridge was what held its fold together at high temperature; once the reducing agent breaks it, the enzyme is held only by weak bonds and unfolds at about the same temperatures as the normal enzyme. At 25 °C neither enzyme unfolds, and the extra bridge holds the chain in the same working shape rather than changing it, so both keep nearly all their activity.
